data.title: UK and EU strike post-Brexit reset deal, but tuition fee row remains unresolved
data.description:
The United Kingdom and the European Union have concluded negotiations on a series of agreements covering food and drink standards, emissions trading and youth mobility, marking a significant step towards resetting relations more than a decade after Brexit.

Downing Street confirmed on Friday that both sides had agreed on implementation timelines for a sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) agreement, a link between their emissions trading systems and a youth mobility scheme.

However, negotiations over tuition fees for European students attending British universities remain unresolved.

“The deal is done – negotiations have concluded,” a No 10 spokesperson said, adding that the two sides would now work towards implementing the agreements.

“Now, both sides will work towards implementation of the youth mobility scheme, the SPS deal and the emissions trading scheme. Both sides have agreed when these will come into force. And those dates are set out in the joint statement, which will be published in due course."

“As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place. And talks will continue on some areas – these will be set out in the joint statement later.”

The announcement came as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham attended his first formal summit with the European Union in Brussels, where he met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa.

Burnham said the broader package could add 0.5% to Britain's economy, while improving trading conditions for businesses and potentially easing pressure on consumers.

During the summit, he described the agreements as “a landmark agreement” that “will benefit every single person in the United Kingdom, but I would say in the European Union too,” according to the Press Association.

“For people struggling with the cost of living, this agreement holds out the real prospect that the cost of the weekly shop will begin to come down and Britain’s big supermarkets are saying that,” he said.

“For businesses struggling with the cost of doing business, this agreement will begin to reduce red tape and make it easier to do business and to export and that is good news for them.”

Food standards agreement expected to reduce trade barriers

A central component of the reset is an agreement to reduce regulatory checks and paperwork on the movement of animals, plants and related products between the UK and the EU.

Under the sanitary and phytosanitary agreement, Britain will align with EU agrifood standards, allowing agricultural and food products to move across borders with fewer checks and administrative requirements.

The arrangement is expected to take effect in 2028, according to multiple draft statements, and is estimated to deliver £5.1 billion ($6.7 billion) in economic benefits to the UK.

The agreement could provide relief to British food producers, exporters and retailers that have faced additional costs and administrative hurdles since the country left the EU's single market.

UK and EU agree to link emissions trading systems

The two sides have also reached an agreement to link their respective emissions trading systems, another important element of the post-Brexit reset.

The arrangement is intended to improve coordination between the UK and EU carbon markets and reduce additional costs for businesses operating across both jurisdictions.

However, the agreement will not immediately exempt British companies from the EU's carbon border taxes.

Overnight briefings indicated that the exemption would only take effect in 2028.

The development is particularly relevant for industries with significant carbon emissions and exposure to European trade, including steel, cement and other energy-intensive manufacturing sectors.

Linking the systems could help reduce regulatory differences and provide businesses with greater certainty as they navigate increasingly stringent climate-related trade requirements.

Youth mobility scheme to allow 100,000 people into UK annually

Another significant outcome of the negotiations is an agreement on a youth experience scheme (YES), which will allow young people to live and work in the UK and EU for a fixed period through lower-cost visas.

The proposed arrangement will allow up to 100,000 people annually to enter the UK, provided they are under the age of 32.

The scheme represents a limited relaxation of restrictions on movement introduced after Brexit, although it does not restore the freedom of movement that existed when Britain was part of the EU.

It is expected to create opportunities for young people seeking international work experience, education and cultural exchanges.

Burnham also highlighted cooperation on illegal immigration, pointing to Britain's participation in the Channel action plan.

“For people worried about illegal immigration, and there are many people who have very legitimate concerns about that, they will be pleased, I’m sure, to hear about Britain’s participation in the Channel action plan and that is a very significant step forward, sharing more data between us on that very important issue,” he said.

Tuition fees remain the biggest sticking point

Despite progress on the broader package, negotiations over tuition fees for European students studying in Britain remain unresolved.

The European Union has been pushing for students studying abroad to receive “equal treatment with nationals as regards tuition fees”, effectively requiring universities to charge EU students the same rates as domestic students.

Britain, however, has proposed an intermediate arrangement that would reduce fees without extending full home-fee status to European students.

According to two EU diplomats granted anonymity to discuss the negotiations, London has so far offered tuition fees of around £12,000, Politico reported.

That would represent a substantial reduction from the average £22,000 currently paid by EU students in Britain, although some courses charge considerably more.

It would also remain above the £9,790 paid by British students, the publication said.

The EU has raised concerns about the proposed arrangement because the fee reduction would be reciprocal.

One diplomat said it could require all 27 member states to introduce a separate tuition fee category for British students, Politico said.

Such a change could prove complicated, potentially requiring legislative amendments and adjustments to university funding systems in individual countries.

The disagreement has therefore emerged as one of the more difficult issues in an otherwise largely successful round of negotiations.

Nevertheless, both sides remain keen to present the agreements as a positive step in rebuilding relations and have expressed confidence that a compromise on tuition fees can eventually be reached.

For Britain, the agreements represent an attempt to secure some of the economic and administrative benefits of closer European integration without reversing its decision to leave the bloc.

The coming years will determine whether the reset translates into lower trade costs, stronger investment and a more predictable relationship between the two sides.

data.title: GTA VI rakes in $2.3B in record opening day: what next for Take-Two stock
data.description:
Grand Theft Auto VI generated over $2.3 billion in sales on its opening day, shattering entertainment industry records on the occasion of its much-awaited release.

GTA 6 released on Thursday worldwide, ending a 13-year wait for fans for the latest edition of the highly successful franchise.

Rockstar Games and parent company Take-Two Interactive TTWO are yet to officially release the sales numbers but estimates suggest that it is already the biggest launch in the entertainment industry ever.

GTA 6 shatters record

Analytics firm Sensor Tower reported that pre-orders and first-day purchases totaled more than 24.5 million units for GTA 6, helping the makers rake in an estimated $2.36 billion on the launch day.

The numbers also include pre-orders that had already topped $1.6 billion before launch.

The latest sales are three times the roughly $800 million generated by GTA V on its 2013 debut.

For context, the highest-grossing movie of all time, Avengers: Endgame, minted roughly $2.94 billion in its lifetime.

Sensor Tower’s estimates, based on platform data and receipt tracking, said that three-quarters of sales were on PlayStation 5, with the remainder on Xbox Series X|S.

Analysts from Niko Partners, a gaming market research firm, expect the game to push past $3 billion in sales this year alone.

Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick has already said that demand was far above the company’s initial expectations.

Near-perfect reviews

GTA 6 makers took over a decade to launch the game after the fifth iteration of the game and spent over $1 billion to develop it.

The hard work is being appreciated by critics who delivered near-universal acclaim.

GTA VI earned a Metacritic score of 99, tying The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the highest aggregate rating in the site’s history and earning “Universal Acclaim” status from more than 150 reviews, all positive.

IGN's Luke Reilly termed GTA 6 the "single most impressive video game I have ever played."

He praised the real-world nature of the game, saying that "this is a world that feels more lived in and real than anything I've ever played."

Forbes' Paul Tassi was amazed by the game and said that "no studio is remotely close to something of this depth and scale."

He also found the video game to be the most impressive thing he has ever played.

What next for Take-Two stock

Take-Two shares rose sharply on Wednesday as early reviews landed but slipped nearly 4% on launch day itself, closing lower amid a broader market pullback.

The stock remains well below recent highs and is down for the year despite the GTA VI catalyst.

Wall Street largely remains constructive. Consensus ratings lean Strong Buy, with several firms raising unit and bookings forecasts.

Wells Fargo, for example, lifted its full-year unit estimate significantly higher.

The firm projected fiscal 2027 net bookings of $9.76 billion, about 19% above the top of Take-Two's own guidance range of $8.0 billion to $8.2 billion.

Bank of America has said the game's release could be a growth-driving catalyst for Take-Two Interactive.

It estimates that GTA 6 needs to generate at least $1.9 billion in sales to meet investor expectations for fiscal 2027.

The brokerage has maintained a Buy rating on Take-Two, with a price target of $330, implying approximately 63% upside from current levels.

Investors will now focus on the longevity of the single-player title, the timing and monetization potential of GTA Online integration, a future PC release, and Take-Two’s upcoming fiscal results that will capture the launch quarter.

Industry analysts are expecting the PC launch and online mode in 2027.

data.title: Why did Anthropic’s IPO fail to boost the AI trade, and what comes next?
data.description:
Anthropic's historic initial public offering, the largest in US history, delivered a major victory for the artificial intelligence company and its investors.

However, it failed to achieve another objective that market participants had hoped for: reviving investor enthusiasm for the broader AI trade.

Anthropic shares (ANT) closed 17% above their IPO price of $83, after opening 34% higher, demonstrating strong demand for the company's stock.

Yet the gains did little to lift sentiment across technology markets, which remained under pressure.

The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.25%, while the S&P 500 declined 2.3% to 7,175.83, reflecting a broader retreat from risk assets.

The weakness extended into Asian markets on Friday, with semiconductor-heavy exchanges bearing the brunt of the selling.

Taiwanese stocks fell 6.7% on Friday, reaching their lowest level since mid-April.

The decline pushed their weekly losses beyond 16%, putting the market on track for its worst five-day rout since 1990.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the country's largest and most valuable listed company, fell approximately 5%.

South Korean equities also declined more than 5%, reaching their lowest levels in more than nine months.

Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix dropped approximately 7% and 6%, respectively.

Anthropic shares themselves came under pressure after the closing bell, falling 6% in pre-market trading to $91.35, below their lowest level during the previous session.

The IPO came at a time when the beating heart of the AI trade-Nvidia, is facing questions over its leadership crisis which has severely impacted its stock, while investors have broadly grown more cautious about AI, increasing scrutiny of expenditure on AI infrastructure to assess whether it is delivering commensurate returns.

The victory of Democrats in recent midterms also spooked markets that it will lead to slower data construction in the country, disrupting the flow of business and revenue.

Nvidia and AMD concerns compound pressure on technology stocks

Several company-specific developments added to Anthropic's inability to lift the AI trade.

Concerns around Nvidia amid concerns about its China exposure and questions surrounding its leadership following the recent espionage scandal seemed to have persisted and continued pressuring the stock.

"There are still a lot of questions over Nvidia, not just when it comes to Chinese spying and minor issues like US national security, but over what Jensen Huang’s departure means for future AI financing," David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation wrote in a note on Thursday.

There are concerns that Nvidia may be less aggressive when it comes to funding new infrastructure projects, and that in turn could apply the brakes across all AI-adjacent corporations should the buildout slow down.

Senior Market Analyst at Trade Nation
David Morrison

Investors are also assessing the potential implications of Washington's increasingly restrictive approach to advanced semiconductor exports.

Nvidia fell over 3% on Thursday.

Meanwhile, AMD shares fell approximately 8% after Hunterbrook Media, an investigative publication affiliated with short seller Hunterbrook Capital, published a report alleging links between the chipmaker and a blacklisted Chinese company.

The report alleged that Chinese server manufacturer IEIT Systems had incorporated at least six newer versions of AMD's firmware into its products after being placed on the US government's export blacklist.

It also warned that changes to US export regulations could expose AMD to additional restrictions on its international business.

The allegations have added another layer of uncertainty for semiconductor investors, who are already concerned about the potential impact of tighter export controls on companies with significant international operations.

The issue gained further attention after lawmakers released confidential information on Thursday indicating that the Commerce Department had approved the sale of more than 800,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies as of May 11.

The approved shipments reportedly included sales to several companies on the Pentagon's list of Chinese military companies.

Dan Ives sees a panic moment but maintains long-term AI optimism

Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, described the market environment as a "tale of two cities", with Anthropic's successful listing highlighting the continued appetite for AI investments even as technology stocks face a difficult period.

"On one part, Anthropic's a watershed event for tech. The success that you've seen here on the IPO, the appetite you saw institutionally in terms of the roadshow... And this is foundational to the AI buildout. And I think that's just important in terms of this IPO. I do think it lays the groundwork for OpenAI in 2027," he said in an interview with CNBC.

However, Ives acknowledged that the broader technology sector was going through a "dark period", with investors struggling to assess the extent of the current sell-off.

"I think part of it is just Nvidia, the worries about China, you talk about the AMD short report. Investors are trying to just figure out, where the bottom is here. It's a panic moment," he said.

Despite the near-term uncertainty, Ives argued that the underlying investment thesis for AI remained intact.

But it's not stopping. We're less than 15% through the buildout of the AI revolution. Everything Anthropic talks about, that's just a piece of what I view as this foundational bull thesis and is not in any way dented despite what we're seeing.

Partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives
Dan Ives

Market liquidity also a factor

Some market participants believe the weakness in technology stocks is also related to the financing requirements of the AI boom and the liquidity available to investors.

Mohamed A El-Erian, Rene M Kern Professor of Practice at The Wharton School and a noted economist, argued that the divergence between Anthropic's performance and the broader market was partly a consequence of investors reallocating capital.

"For those surprised that the NASDAQ and other US stock market indices are down 1.5–2% (CNBC data below) while Anthropic is trading 20% above its IPO price, remember this isn't just about the promise of AI, but about making room for it," he wrote on X.

"In a narrow sense, investor financing of the mega-IPO involves making room by selling other holdings. In a broader sense, it mirrors what we have been seeing with yields: with no large borrowers reducing their use of the bond market, financing costs rise for everyone, hitting rate-sensitive sectors particularly hard," he wrote.

In other words, the enthusiasm surrounding a major AI listing does not necessarily translate into fresh capital flowing into the entire sector.

Investors may instead be reallocating existing holdings to participate in the IPO, putting pressure on other assets.

Gene Munster, managing partner at Deep Water Management, also argued that the market reaction was not necessarily a reflection of weakening confidence in AI itself.

"Many were betting the Anthropic IPO would lift the broader AI trade. Classic groupthink. My take: Today’s action isn’t an indictment of AI. It’s what happens when many were on the same side of the trade. Investors still want the exposure, and the $80B Anthropic raised will soon fund infrastructure and applications," Munster wrote on X.

His comments suggest that crowded positioning may have contributed to the sharp divergence between Anthropic's listing performance and the wider technology market.

Anthropic's IPO could still benefit semiconductor companies

Despite failing to lift technology stocks immediately, Anthropic's listing could have important implications for the AI infrastructure ecosystem over the longer term.

Gil Luria, head of technology research at DA Davidson, described the IPO as an "important milestone" for the AI sector.

He noted that Anthropic would have more than $230 billion in cash, based on the details of its IPO and its latest financial statements, giving the company considerable financial resources to expand its operations.

"Anthropic now has an enormous war chest it can use to buy more compute from its providers, primarily Amazon, Google and SpaceX. Those companies in turn now have visibility to buy more chips from Broadcom, Nvidia and Micron," Luria told MarketWatch.

Compute refers to the chips and other hardware required to train and operate AI models.

This creates a potential chain of benefits for the broader technology industry.

Anthropic's ability to finance additional computing capacity could translate into greater infrastructure spending by cloud providers, which would subsequently support demand for semiconductors, memory and networking equipment.

The implications could extend beyond Anthropic itself, particularly if other AI companies follow its fundraising and listing trajectory.

However, the immediate market reaction suggests that investors are not yet willing to assume that additional AI spending will automatically translate into higher valuations across the technology sector.

What could the Anthropic IPO mean for the AI trade in 2027?

The outlook for AI stocks will depend on whether companies can demonstrate that their substantial investments in computing infrastructure are generating sustainable financial returns.

According to Saxo, its base case for the broader AI trade through the end of the year is one of choppy stabilisation and selective rebounds, rather than a return to indiscriminate buying.

"Some crowded positioning has already been reduced. If bond yields stabilise and liquidity conditions improve, quality AI companies with resilient earnings and strong balance sheets could benefit from renewed interest," wrote Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo.

However, she cautioned that a sustained recovery would require greater confidence in the financial returns generated by AI investments.

"But a broad and durable recovery would require greater confidence in the returns generated by AI spending."

That distinction could become increasingly important as the industry moves into 2027.

The AI investment cycle is entering a phase in which the ability to raise capital and secure computing capacity may not be enough to sustain valuations.

Anthropic's IPO has demonstrated that institutional investors remain willing to commit substantial capital to companies at the centre of the AI revolution.

Its success could also encourage other private AI companies, including OpenAI, to explore public listings.

However, the broader market's reaction shows that enthusiasm for individual AI companies does not necessarily translate into confidence in the entire ecosystem.

For semiconductor manufacturers, cloud providers and other infrastructure companies, the next phase of the AI trade may depend less on announcements of fresh spending and more on evidence that the investments are producing measurable returns.

data.title: Trump, Xi and Putin promise peace, but what changes for defence stocks?
data.description:
US defence stocks face renewed scrutiny after President Donald Trump joined Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in a peace declaration, although their agreement contained no binding arms reductions or changes to military budgets.

The three leaders met in Shenzhen on Thursday and pledged talks on lowering nuclear risks. The declaration offered no settlement of the wars in Ukraine or Iran.

For Lockheed Martin, RTX and Northrop Grumman, the more immediate question is whether Congress will support Trump's proposed $1.5 trillion defence budget for fiscal 2027.

Lockheed Martin and RTX fell on Thursday, while Northrop Grumman was little changed.

Trump Xi Putin peace summit: A declaration without cuts to military spending

The joint statement committed Washington, Beijing and Moscow to discussing nuclear risk reduction and preventing proliferation. It also addressed United Nations reform and stable energy supplies.

It did not commit any country to reducing its arsenal, cancelling weapons programmes or changing procurement plans.

That distinction matters for defence contractors. An arms-control agreement could ultimately alter demand for certain systems, but a diplomatic statement leaves existing contracts and military requirements intact.

"The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction," Brookings Institution expert Patricia Kim told The Guardian, also pointing to efforts to prevent proliferation.

The meeting could open a channel for negotiations. It does not resolve the strategic rivalries that have prompted governments to replenish weapons stocks, expand missile defences and modernise nuclear forces.

Investors therefore have little basis for treating Thursday's declaration as an immediate reduction in the industry's order pipeline.

US defence stocks: Record backlogs offer support, but not immunity

Lockheed Martin reported third-quarter sales of $20.7 billion, up from $18.6 billion a year earlier. Its backlog reached a record $292 billion, supported by programmes including the F-35 and missile interceptors.

RTX reported a $340 billion backlog, although $176 billion of that represented commercial aerospace rather than defence orders. Its defence backlog totalled $164 billion, reflecting demand for missiles and air-defence systems.

Northrop Grumman ended September with $109.6 billion in backlog. Its B-21 bomber and Sentinel missile programmes remain important elements of US nuclear modernisation.

Those commitments provide revenue visibility, but backlogs are not the same as immediate sales or guaranteed margins. Production delays, costs and programme reviews still affect profitability.

Portfolio manager Katerina Kosmopoulou said defence shares had "lost momentum in recent months", citing expensive valuations, political uncertainty and hopes of conflict resolution, according to MoneyWeek.

Even a more peaceful diplomatic environment would not automatically eliminate stockpile replenishment or long-running weapons contracts.

US defence spending matters more than summit promises

Trump wants $1.5 trillion in defence funding for fiscal 2027, compared with approximately $901 billion approved for 2026. His request combines $1.15 trillion in discretionary spending with another $350 billion intended through reconciliation.

After Democrats made gains in the midterm elections, approval of the full package looks uncertain. Jefferies analysts expect an outcome nearer $1.15 trillion.

TD Cowen analyst Roman Schweizer warned earlier this month that Trump-branded programmes were "dead" politically, singling out risks to initiatives such as Golden Dome and Golden Fleet.

He regarded nuclear modernisation, including Northrop's B-21 and Sentinel, as comparatively better protected.

The proposed rise also raises questions about how quickly contractors could turn new funding into production.

Missile factories, aircraft assembly lines and specialist suppliers cannot necessarily expand at the pace politicians promise.

Lawmakers face a government funding deadline on 11 December, making budget negotiations a nearer-term catalyst than the Shenzhen statement.

data.title: SpaceX stock: why are lenders trying to stop Elon Musk's AI space plans?
data.description:
SpaceX faces fresh questions over its artificial intelligence expansion after lenders backing a reported $43 billion financing package sought assurances that Elon Musk would not launch the Nvidia chips securing the debt into orbit.

The proposed restrictions, reported by the Financial Times on Friday, reflect concerns that valuable computing equipment would be difficult to recover if SpaceX defaulted. Whether the provisions entered the final agreements remains unclear.

SpaceX stock (NASDAQ: SPCX) closed 3.53% lower at $138.43 on Thursday, before the lender concerns were widely reported.

The dispute highlights a growing tension between Musk's plans for orbital data centres and the practical demands of financing AI infrastructure.

SpaceX stock: Why lenders want Nvidia chips to stay on Earth

The financing, known as Project Saturn, supports the purchase of Nvidia processors for SpaceX's expanding AI business.

Investors bought more than $30 billion of debt on Thursday, with Bloomberg reporting a roughly $32 billion bond sale.

The largest portion is a $25 billion investment-grade bond backed by approximately five years of lease payments for the GPUs.

The new securities reportedly yield about 8.3%, compared with roughly 7.2% on SpaceX debt maturing in 2031.

The structure offers lenders security in the underlying chips and contractual payments. But servers launched into orbit would be far harder to repossess, transport or sell after a default than equipment installed in a terrestrial data centre.

Rapid advances in semiconductor technology also mean their collateral value could diminish before the debt matures, heightening the importance of physical access.

"The SpaceX GPU deal appears cleverly structured," Shorecliff Asset Management chief investment officer Grant Nachman told the Financial Times, identifying potential demand from insurers seeking higher-yielding investment-grade debt.

Elon Musk's orbital data centres face an engineering test

Musk wants to place powerful computing systems aboard satellites, potentially using solar energy in orbit to support AI workloads without some of the land and electricity constraints facing Earth-based facilities.

Doing so would introduce problems conventional data centres rarely confront. Heat must be radiated into space, components must survive radiation and extreme conditions, and faulty equipment cannot readily be replaced.

Communications capacity and the cost of launch add further uncertainty.

Reusable Starship rockets could eventually make carrying substantial hardware into orbit more affordable.

SpaceX made progress in its November test programme, although the heavy-lift system has not established routine, economical reuse.

“Starship remains the enabling infrastructure” behind major opportunities, including orbital data centres and expanded Starlink deployments, KeyBanc analyst Mike Leshock told MarketWatch.

For now, SpaceX says its Apollo-backed GPU arrangement is intended for terrestrial computing.

That difference matters: financing assets in orbit may require protections fundamentally different from those supporting ordinary equipment leases.

What the financing dispute means for SpaceX stock

In October, SpaceX announced a binding commitment for an approximately $40 billion equipment lease with an Apollo-managed entity.

Deliveries of Nvidia Vera Rubin systems are expected to begin during the first half of 2027, subject to closing conditions.

The earlier lease and the reported $43 billion financing describe related arrangements, not two separate sums to be added together.

Investors remain divided on how much value to assign SpaceX's emerging AI business.

Morgan Stanley analyst Adam Jonas reiterated an Overweight rating and $300 price target, with $170 of that target attributed to enterprise AI, according to TheStreet.

"On FY28, SPCX trades cheaper than the S&P500. Interesting," Jonas wrote in an earlier valuation note.

By contrast, Morningstar estimates fair value at $70, reflecting concerns about infrastructure spending and whether AI demand can justify the investment.

data.title: Oil price today: Brent pares losses after sliding to $90.06 amid Hormuz tensions
data.description:
Oil prices recovered from their session lows on Friday as traders weighed renewed security threats in the Strait of Hormuz against rising crude inventories and expectations of a global supply surplus.

January Brent futures were down 0.61% at $91.42 a barrel at 11:55 GMT, after briefly falling to $90.06 earlier in London trading. The contract settled at $91.98 on Thursday.

Actively traded January West Texas Intermediate futures slipped 0.25% to $82.23.

The partial recovery left Brent heading for a third consecutive weekly decline, highlighting the market's increasingly muted response to geopolitical threats.

What happened to oil prices today?

Iran's Revolutionary Guard navy claimed on Thursday that two supertankers carrying more than 4 million barrels of crude had struck mines and caught fire while navigating the Strait of Hormuz.

The vessels were not identified, and the alleged mine strikes remain independently unverified.

The Joint Maritime Information Center said in its latest advisory that no official or national authorities had confirmed Iran's claims.

However, the organisation documented four separate attacks in the strait over the preceding four days.

Among them was Wednesday's incident involving a tanker struck by an unidentified projectile near Khasab, Oman. The crew was reported safe.

Regional tensions intensified further on Friday when the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted five drones and a ballistic missile targeting the kingdom.

Despite those developments, Brent surrendered its initial gains, suggesting traders were reluctant to price in substantial additional supply losses without evidence of a sustained disruption.

Why did oil prices fall, then recover?

Oil's decline came alongside broader weakness in commodities.

The US dollar index traded around 103.89, close to its recent 19-month high, while gold and silver also recorded sharp losses.

Dollar strength makes crude more expensive for buyers using other currencies, potentially weakening demand.

Meanwhile, official US data showed commercial crude inventories increased by 3.4 million barrels to 417.8 million in the week ended 13 November.

Goldman Sachs oil researcher Daan Struyven has argued that exporters have become increasingly effective at managing the disruption through alternative pipelines, escorted shipping and ship-to-ship transfers.

Additional production outside the Persian Gulf and weaker Chinese demand have also helped soften the impact.

Goldman estimates the oil market moved into surplus in October and expects the excess to reach approximately 2 million barrels a day next year.

That supply outlook has made it harder for geopolitical developments alone to sustain a rally.

Can Brent hold above $90 before the OPEC+ meeting?

Goldman expects Brent to average $88 a barrel in 2027 before declining towards $78 late that year.

Its forecast assumes no major escalation causing lasting damage to Middle Eastern energy infrastructure.

The next important policy event comes on 29 November, when OPEC+ ministers meet to consider production arrangements for 2027.

Friday also marks the expiry of December WTI futures, making January the more actively traded contract.

Investors will additionally monitor the University of Michigan's final November consumer sentiment survey for clues about US economic demand and inflation expectations.

For those comparing the best commodity trading platforms, Friday's volatility illustrates why longer-term supply forecasts and immediate geopolitical risks need to be considered separately.

data.title: Nvidia's legal troubles mount as California AG and House Democrats launch probes
data.description:
Democratic lawmakers have launched an investigation into Nvidia, while California Attorney General Rob Bonta has issued an investigative subpoena to the chipmaker, adding further to the legal pressure against the chipmaking giant.

The scrutiny follows allegations involving Huang’s reported relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence and connected to Singapore-based cloud firm Megaspeed, which is under investigation.

Huang resigned from his role as CEO and President of the company last week as he continues to face scrutiny over his actions.

Investigators are looking into possible national security risks involving advanced AI chips, as well as whether Nvidia properly informed investors about the matter.

Nvidia shares hit a fresh 52-week low on Thursday after falling 3.3% in the session. The stock was down over 2% in premarket trading on Friday.

House Democrats seek Nvidia records

Two Democratic members of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Representatives Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California and Gregory Meeks of New York, have written to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick seeking records of communications between Nvidia and the office responsible for investigating chip smuggling.

The lawmakers want to know whether Nvidia tried to influence an investigation into Megaspeed, where Alice Huang served as an executive.

Megaspeed has been under investigation by the US authortiies for two years. The firm has denied any wrongdoing and pledged to cooperate with the probe.

"The American public and Congress deserve a full accounting of what happened," US Representatives Gregory ​Meeks, ranking member ​of the House ⁠Committee on Foreign Affairs, and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California wrote in the letter.

The lawmakers have requested answers and relevant documents by December 1.

The letter also says they wanted to know "whether the department allowed a major American corporation that is financially and ​personally linked to the Trump administration to interfere with enforcement activity."

California AG issues subpoena

California Attorney General Rob Bonta served Nvidia with an investigative subpoena on Thursday.

His office is looking into whether the company’s advanced chips or confidential information reached China, and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public about the risks.

“The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said in a statement.

“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” Bonta said.

“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” the attorney general said.

Congressional hearings await

The investigations are also moving forward in Congress.

Huang is scheduled to give a transcribed interview on December 1 before the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party. Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter is due to appear the following day.

Legal troubles do not end here.

Investor Mark Kistenmacher has filed a proposed shareholder class-action lawsuit against Nvidia and Huang in the US District Court for the Northern District of California in San Francisco.

The lawsuit alleges that the company and its former CEO made misleading statements or withheld information about the relationship with Alice Huang and the associated risks.

It seeks to represent shareholders who bought Nvidia stock during a specified period and suffered losses as a result.

“Several hundreds of investors have contacted us and expressed an interest to join the case — investors of all walks of life, from mom and pops to investors with very large losses,” attorney Phil Kim at Rosen Law Firm, which represents the investor, told CNBC.

data.title: Nasdaq futures tumble 360 points: 5 things to know before Wall Street opens
data.description:
US stock futures fell on Friday as investors sought refuge in Treasuries after Wall Street's sell-off, while contrasting earnings from Intuit and Gap highlighted an uneven corporate outlook.

Nasdaq 100 futures dropped 1.15%, or 360 points, while S&P 500 and Dow contracts lost 0.5% and 0.1%.

The losses followed Thursday's 1,101-point Dow slump and a 2.02% fall in the S&P 500.

A retreat in government bond yields pointed to demand for safety, despite bets on higher Federal Reserve rates.

5 things to know before Wall Street opens

1. Intuit slides as Mailchimp sale exposes growth concerns

Shares in the TurboTax and QuickBooks owner tumbled roughly 10% in pre-market trading despite quarterly revenue rising 12% to $4.35 billion and adjusted earnings reaching $2.91 a share.

Intuit agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion, versus roughly $12 billion paid in 2021.

It also lowered its fiscal 2027 sales forecast to $23.08 billion–$23.37 billion, reflecting weaker expectations for Credit Karma.

Management plans to use the cash proceeds for buybacks once the deal closes in early 2027.

2. Gap rises, but its consumer warning tempers enthusiasm

The clothing retailer gained around 3%–4% following adjusted quarterly earnings of 82 cents a share, ahead of the 78-cent analyst estimate.

Sales rose 2% to approximately $4 billion. Its namesake brand posted 9% comparable-sales growth, while Old Navy was flat and Athleta remained weak.

Gap nevertheless reduced its full-year adjusted earnings forecast to $2.29–$2.34 a share, citing a slower start to the holiday quarter.

BJ's Wholesale Club reports before Friday's opening bell, providing another snapshot of shoppers looking for value amid pressure on discretionary spending.

3. Treasury yields drop even as rate-hike bets persist

The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield fell towards 4.99%, slipping below 5%, while the two-year yield moved towards 4.71% as demand for government debt strengthened.

Yields fall when bond prices rise.

Capital.com strategist Daniela Hathorn linked the shift to investors seeking safer assets amid a broad equity retreat, despite hawkish Fed expectations.

The move presents an important distinction: falling yields can reflect anxiety about growth, not necessarily confidence that policy easing is imminent.

4. Monthly options expiry raises the prospect of choppy trading

Friday marks November's scheduled expiration for standard monthly US equity and index options.

Traders may close contracts, roll exposure into later maturities or rebalance hedges as expiry approaches.

Those adjustments can raise volumes and produce abrupt moves around widely watched index levels, particularly after Thursday's broad sell-off.

The impact is not automatically negative: dealer positioning and the balance of buying and selling determine whether hedging amplifies or dampens swings.

5. Sentiment survey and Fed speeches provide the day's macro test

The University of Michigan releases its final November consumer sentiment index at 10 am Eastern, after a preliminary reading of 51.0, up from October's 48.0.

Investors will examine households' inflation expectations as closely as confidence itself.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller is scheduled to speak at 8:25 am, with Governor Lisa Cook following at 12:15 pm.

Remarks suggesting inflation is proving stubborn could renew pressure on stocks, while signs of softer consumer demand may reinforce concerns about growth.

data.title: Interview: Could tokenized stocks be the next stablecoins? Flowdesk CEO answers
data.description:
Tokenization is moving from industry experiments towards becoming part of traditional financial infrastructure.

As banks and asset managers explore bringing government bonds, money market funds and equities on-chain, the challenge is no longer simply issuing digital representations of existing assets.

Institutions must also rethink custody, settlement, collateral management and liquidity.

Invezz spoke with Guilhem Chaumont, CEO and co-founder of Flowdesk, about what is driving this shift, whether tokenized equities can replicate the growth of stablecoins, and where the strongest institutional demand is emerging.

He argues that tokenized securities could make assets more useful across venues and time zones, but warns that continuous trading does not guarantee continuous liquidity.

The bigger hurdle may be banks' willingness to rebuild legacy operations and assume new forms of risk. The conversation examines what must change before on-chain markets can operate at scale.

Invezz: Tokenization has been discussed for years, but the industry now appears to be moving towards more practical institutional applications. What has changed over the past 12–18 months, and are we finally approaching a meaningful turning point?

Three years ago, only a handful of institutions called tokenisation the future, and today, it is the consensus, showing how far the conversation has moved.

The technology has truly leapfrogged between 2020 and 2023.

Over the past 18 months, firms such as BlackRock and Securitize have built tools that let any institution mint and redeem without friction.

The next phase is adoption, where institutions have to rebuild their middle and back offices to settle onchain, and it will take significant time.

Once a few of them move at scale, the efficiency gap will force everyone else to follow, and I think we are two to four years out from that point.

The clearest signal for me is that banks kept investing time and money through one of the weakest trading stretches crypto has seen, so their interest has nothing to do with price.

Invezz: You’ve said tokenized stocks could follow stablecoins over the next four to five years. Stablecoins grew because they solved a real problem. What problem does a tokenized equity solve that an ordinary brokerage account doesn’t?

A brokerage account serves a US investor trading in US hours well.

The shares it holds, though, sit within a single intermediary's ledger and settle T+1, and they have little use beyond being bought, held, or sold.

A tokenised equity settles in minutes and can move across venues and jurisdictions.

That means an investor in Dubai or Singapore can access it through platforms they already use, and an institution can post it as collateral or use it in DeFi outside market hours.

Stablecoins followed the same path, evolving from a tool just for crypto traders to settlement infrastructure used by payment firms and corporates well outside crypto.

I expect equities to follow that arc over the next four to five years.

Invezz: Beyond equities, which traditional asset classes stand to benefit most from tokenization over the next few years? Is the bigger opportunity in making already-liquid assets such as government bonds and money market funds more useful for collateral and settlement, or in bringing traditionally illiquid assets on-chain? Where do you see the strongest commercial demand?

The strongest demand today is for those assets that already trade in deep markets, such as government bonds, money market funds, or ETFs.

Their pricing is already established, so tokenisation adds value by making them more useful as collateral and in settlement.

A tokenised money market fund can be pledged as collateral with a trading counterparty at any time, weekends included, and it keeps earning yield while pledged.

A treasury team no longer has to hold idle cash against its positions, and that is where institutions are committing their budgets now.

Real estate and private credit will follow, but over a far longer horizon than the market assumes, because tokenising an illiquid asset does not immediately create demand for it.

Invezz: Are we seeing genuine migration of financial market activity on-chain, or is tokenization primarily becoming a new settlement layer for existing markets? What would need to change for institutions to move execution and price discovery on-chain as well?

For now, tokenisation is mostly a settlement layer.

A tokenised US stock still takes its price from the primary exchange, and onchain venues track that price while the exchange is open.

Execution and price discovery will move onchain only when three conditions are met.

First, onchain liquidity has to be deep enough for prices set there to lead the market.

Second, regulators have to accept stablecoins as fiat equivalents for the cash end of a trade.

Lastly, institutions have to rebuild their back offices so that onchain settlement becomes their default.

Even then, I expect the structure to resemble US equities today, where roughly half of volume trades off exchange.

Public venues still set the reference price, while large or complex trades go through counterparties that keep them private from the market but fully visible to the regulator.

Invezz: Of the five factors – regulation, custody, settlement, liquidity and institutional risk appetite – which do you see as the most significant barriers to greater institutional participation? Looking ahead to 2027, which of these do you think will take the longest to address, even as progress is made on the others?

Regulation draws most of the attention in this industry, but regulators, for instance in Europe and the UAE, are already moving at commercial speed.

The barrier that will take the longest to resolve is institutional risk appetite, which depends on confidence in custody and on how quickly banks can rebuild their operations.

The questions institutions ask us have rarely changed in three years.

They ask whether they can tokenise a billion dollars, what the process involves, and whether, once the regulator signs off, they are comfortable holding that onchain.

No regulation answers those questions on its own, which is why I expect risk appetite to trail the other factors well into 2027.

Invezz: Round-the-clock trading is frequently presented as one of tokenization’s biggest advantages. But continuous trading does not necessarily mean continuous liquidity, particularly when underlying assets trade in traditional markets with fixed operating hours. Is there genuine institutional demand for 24/7 trading in tokenized equities and funds, and who ultimately takes on the price risk and inventory costs when traditional markets are closed?

Continuous trading and continuous liquidity are starkly different things, as anyone buying a tokenised equity on a Saturday afternoon will tell you.

The demand is real nonetheless. It comes from investors in time zones outside US trading hours, and from crypto-native funds that trade around the clock and want to use these assets as collateral alongside the rest of their holdings.

When the underlying market is closed, the liquidity provider carries the price risk and the inventory until that market reopens and it can hedge.

It then prices that risk into a wider spread. This way, clients can still trade while the underlying market is shut, at a price that reflects the risk involved.

Banks that want to offer weekend access can rely on a counterparty already running 24/7 liquidity rather than building that capability themselves.

data.title: Solana price struggles despite major upgrade: is another sell-off coming?
data.description:
Solana (SOL) faces growing downside pressure as institutional selling, setbacks involving proposed exchange-traded funds (ETFs), and weak technical indicators continue to weigh on investor sentiment.

The cryptocurrency's near-term outlook has become increasingly uncertain following CoinShares' disclosure that it reduced its Solana treasury holdings during October.

SOL remains vulnerable to further losses unless buying demand improves and the cryptocurrency reclaims important resistance levels.

CoinShares sells half of Solana holdings to fund share buyback

Institutional selling has emerged as a concern for Solana following CoinShares' latest treasury disclosure.

CoinShares sold its entire Ethereum treasury position and approximately half of its Solana holdings during October.

The Solana transactions generated around $2.7 million, with proceeds directed toward financing a share buyback program.

The decision reduced the company's direct exposure to both cryptocurrencies, although the sales were associated with corporate capital allocation rather than necessarily reflecting a negative long-term assessment of the assets.

Nevertheless, the disclosure has attracted attention amid broader weakness in the cryptocurrency market.

Meanwhile, Roundhill's decision to withdraw its planned Solana and XRP income ETFs has raised additional questions about demand for new cryptocurrency investment products.

Roundhill's withdrawal suggests that launching new cryptocurrency income products remains challenging under current market conditions.

The development also comes as competing products reportedly attracted only around $12 million, highlighting limited demand for this particular category of investment vehicles.

Still, the decision could weigh on sentiment by reducing expectations for additional investment channels in the near term.

These developments come despite Solana reaching an important technical milestone with the official launch of Solana 1.0, marking its transition away from the mainnet beta designation.

The blockchain officially transitioned from its long-running mainnet beta designation to Solana 1.0. It marks a new stage in the network's evolution and signals progress in its operational maturity.

Solana has spent years developing its infrastructure to support high-throughput transactions, decentralized applications, and blockchain-based financial services.

Moving beyond the beta designation represents an important milestone for the network's technical development and public positioning. 

However, the transition does not automatically guarantee improved market performance or eliminate operational risks.

Solana technical outlook: SOL remains below key moving averages as sellers dominate

Solana's technical indicators continue to suggest that sellers maintain control of the market. At press time on Friday, SOL/USD trades below several important moving averages across hourly and daily timeframes.

The hourly 20-period Simple Moving Average (SMA-20) stands near $73.47, while the hourly SMA-50 is positioned around $73.87. Meanwhile, the daily 200-period SMA sits significantly higher at $88.65.

Trading below these indicators suggests that both short-term and longer-term momentum remain weak.

The hourly trendline at $73.62 also represents immediate resistance. A sustained recovery above this level could provide an early indication that buying pressure is improving.

However, SOL would still need to reclaim additional moving averages to demonstrate a more convincing shift in momentum.

Other technical indicators reinforce the bearish outlook. The Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) remains negative, suggesting that downward momentum continues to dominate.

The RSI of 24 means that Solana is still in the oversold region. The Average Directional Index (ADX), when considered alongside bearish directional signals, supports the view that the prevailing downtrend remains established.

Meanwhile, negative Bull/Bear Power readings indicate that sellers retain an advantage during intraday trading.

Nevertheless, the broader technical picture remains bearish until SOL begins reclaiming important resistance levels.

If the bearish trend persists, the $64.20 level represents the immediate support level on the daily timeframe. 

A sustained breakdown below this region could encourage additional selling and increase the risk of a deeper correction.

Until SOL reclaims important moving averages, potential rebounds may remain corrective rather than signaling a sustained bullish reversal.
